questions.question: What is the core correctness invariant of a production stream processor?
options: Every event must be processed in under one millisecond
Accepted events update bounded, recoverable state according to an explicit time and delivery contract
All events must share one global ordering key
The processor must keep all history in memory
questions.explanation: Latency is useful only when the result remains correct under delay, duplication, bursts, and recovery. Bounded state plus explicit time and delivery semantics define that contract.

questions.question: A group has 12 partitions and 18 consumers. How many consumers can actively own partitions at once?
questions.explanation: Within one consumer group, an active partition is owned by one consumer. Consumers beyond the 12 partitions wait idle.

questions.question: Input is 120,000 events/s and processing capacity is 150,000 events/s. A 60-second outage creates 7.2 million queued events. How long does catch-up take after recovery?
options: 48 seconds
60 seconds
240 seconds
600 seconds
questions.explanation: Spare capacity is 30,000 events/s. Dividing 7.2 million queued events by 30,000 events/s gives 240 seconds.

questions.question: What does an event-time watermark assert?
options: No older event can ever arrive
The broker has deleted every older event
Event time has probably advanced far enough to finalize results under the lateness policy
Every producer clock is perfectly synchronized
questions.explanation: A watermark is a progress and completeness claim used by the processor. Older events can still arrive and must follow the declared late-event policy.

questions.question: Which design makes at-least-once replay safe for a payment capture sink?
options: Blindly append every retry
Store a stable idempotency key with the business effect
Remove event IDs to reduce payload size
Increase the window size without changing the sink
questions.explanation: At-least-once transport can replay. Persisting a stable idempotency key atomically with the effect turns retries into the same logical operation.

questions.question: What happens when sustained input exceeds processing capacity?
options: Lag grows without bound until input falls or capacity rises
Checkpointing automatically doubles capacity
The watermark guarantees the queue drains
Extra retention makes consumers process faster
questions.explanation: Lag growth is input rate minus processing capacity. Positive sustained growth means the system cannot reach steady state.

questions.question: Which metric most directly reveals a hot partition hidden by healthy aggregate throughput?
options: Cluster-wide average CPU only
Per-partition lag and processing rate
Total topic retention in days
Number of dashboard viewers
questions.explanation: A hot key can saturate one owner while the rest remain idle. Partition-level lag and rate expose that imbalance.

questions.question: Why restore and replay from checkpoints during production readiness testing?
options: To prove the checkpoint is recoverable, measure catch-up, and verify sink deduplication
To avoid defining a retention policy
To guarantee producer clocks are correct
To replace schema compatibility testing
questions.explanation: Checkpoint creation alone does not prove recovery. A restore drill validates state, source positions, replay headroom, and downstream correctness.
